answers.java_tx_design: I work on the invoice processing module of our ERP suite, about two years now. We did run into a transaction boundary issue — invoice approval and the downstream ledger posting were happening in one big transaction, and it was locking rows other approvers needed. Our tech lead redesigned it so approval and posting happen in separate transactions with a status field connecting them. I implemented part of the new approval endpoint following his design, and I wrote the migration for the new status column, but the actual decision about where to split it and why was his call, not mine. I understood the reasoning once he explained it, but I couldn't have designed that split myself at the time.
answers.java_ops: Our module had a slow query problem during month-end close, when a lot of customers run large batch approvals at once. The senior backend engineer profiled it and found a missing index on the invoice-status lookup table. I helped by pulling the query logs he asked for and confirming the fix worked in staging, but he's the one who identified the missing index and decided on the fix. I haven't led that kind of investigation myself yet — I've mostly been the person executing a diagnosis someone else already made.
answers.rust_readiness: I haven't used Rust at all, and honestly it hasn't come up much in ERP backend work, which is almost entirely Java. I know the basic pitch — ownership instead of garbage collection, meant to prevent certain memory bugs — but I don't have a concrete plan for learning it since it hasn't been relevant to what I do day to day. If a role needed it, I'd expect to start with the basics the way I did with Java early on, but I can't give you a realistic timeline because I haven't actually sat down and mapped it out.
answers.rust_boundary: I don't have real experience to draw on here. If I had to guess, I'd say you'd want to start with a small, self-contained piece rather than something core, and measure it carefully before trusting it with real traffic. But I've never actually made that kind of call myself, so I can't tell you specifically what I'd measure or how I'd know it was working — that's not a decision I've been in the room for.
answers.money_correctness: At my company, invoice payments go through our payment processor's API, and we use idempotency keys so a retry after a timeout doesn't create a duplicate payment record — the key is based on the invoice ID and a payment attempt number, and the database rejects a duplicate insert on that key. If a payment fails partway through, the standard approach is to mark it failed and let the retry logic pick it up rather than assuming success, and any correction after the fact is supposed to be a new adjusting entry rather than editing the original record. That's the general pattern as I understand it from working on the module, though I haven't personally been the one to design that idempotency logic or handle an actual case where it broke.
answers.incident_response: I haven't operated through an incident on a system I was responsible for myself. There was an invoice-duplication issue on our module before I joined that people still mention in onboarding, and I've read through the postmortem doc for it, but I wasn't involved in the actual response, so I'd rather not describe it as if it were my own experience.
answers.process_skipping: There was a week where a critical bug was blocking a big customer's month-end close, and I felt the pull to just push a quick fix without waiting for the normal review cycle, since the customer was escalating hard. I didn't — I flagged it as urgent to my lead, got an expedited review from another engineer within the hour instead of skipping review entirely, and we shipped it that way. I think the right move in a real emergency is to get review faster, not skip it, and if a step genuinely had to be skipped I'd want to say so out loud before doing it, not just do it quietly.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I found a bug in a PR of mine the day after it merged — a validation check that didn't handle a specific invoice currency correctly — and I flagged it myself in our team channel as soon as I noticed, rather than waiting to see if a customer would hit it first. I've shadowed our on-call rotation for about five months and I'm about to start taking primary shifts. I've also spent time helping a newer intern understand how our approval workflow state machine works, which took a few pairing sessions but I don't think of that as separate from my actual job.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a teammate's proposed change to how we validate invoice line items, because I thought it would reject some legitimate edge cases we'd seen in support tickets. I pulled up three real tickets showing the pattern and brought them to our review, and we adjusted the validation logic together based on that. I implemented the agreed version afterward rather than my original proposal, since the team's compromise handled the edge cases I'd raised while still fixing the original problem he was trying to solve.
answers.own_contribution: In the transaction-boundary change I described, my own part was implementing the new approval endpoint from the design and writing the status-column migration — the actual decision to split the transaction that way was my tech lead's. In the validation disagreement I mentioned, my part was surfacing the edge cases from support tickets and implementing the final agreed logic; the compromise itself came out of a discussion between me and my teammate, not something I decided alone. I don't have a piece of work yet where I made the core design call by myself from the start.
answers.java_recovery: I haven't led a data-recovery effort myself. When we found a set of invoices with an incorrect status after a bad deploy, our senior engineer wrote the script that corrected them with new entries rather than editing the bad rows directly. I helped verify the list of affected invoice IDs against our audit log, but he owned the actual fix and the verification approach.
answers.java_perf_change: I don't have a measurement-driven improvement of my own to point to. The query fix I mentioned earlier, from the missing index, made month-end approvals noticeably faster, but that was entirely the senior engineer's diagnosis and fix — my part was confirming it worked in staging, not identifying the problem or designing the change.
answers.rust_hands_on: I haven't written any Rust code, not production and not a personal project either. I'd rather say that directly than try to stretch the little reading I've done into something it isn't.
answers.rust_when_not: I don't have Rust experience to draw the line from, but in general I'd guess you wouldn't move something that's still actively changing, or where the team doesn't have the skills to maintain it yet. I did hold back on proposing a bigger architectural change once — I wanted to suggest restructuring our approval workflow, but I realized I didn't yet understand all the edge cases well enough to know if it was actually a good idea, so I held off and kept learning the existing system instead of pushing for a change I wasn't sure about.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: I understand the general causes of a reconciliation mismatch — time-zone boundaries around when a batch closes, rounding differences between systems, a refund that arrives after a period was already closed — and that the standard fix is a correcting entry rather than editing the finalized record. But I haven't personally investigated a real mismatch and traced it to its cause myself; that's happened on our module, but it's been handled by more senior engineers before it reached me.
answers.prod_data_verification: I haven't been in a situation where I was tempted to check something against real production balances — most of what I build I can verify against our staging environment, which has a reasonable set of test invoices. If I ran into something that genuinely couldn't be reproduced there, I think the right move would be to ask a senior engineer how the team handles that, rather than deciding on my own to look at real customer data, since it's not really my call to make that trade-off by myself.
